sentences.text: The hoopoe starling measured 30 centimeters in length.
Its plumage featured white and grey feathers, with darker brown and grey tones covering the back, wings, and tail.
A long, slender, sharp, and frayed tongue likely moved rapidly to help the bird feed on fruit, nectar, pollen, and invertebrates.
Early colonists of Réunion called these birds "huppe" because their crests and curved bills resembled those of the hoopoe.
The only known life drawing of this extinct bird was created by French artist Paul Philippe Sauguin de Jossigny in the early 1770s.
Analysis of a dissected specimen revealed stomach contents containing seeds and berries of Pseudobuxus, possibly Eugenia buxifolia.
The bird was first mentioned in the 17th century and was long believed to be related to the hoopoe.
The earliest potential record is a list from 1658 compiled by French governor Étienne de Flacourt.
The bird likely lived in large flocks within humid areas and marshes.
It was an omnivore that fed on plant matter and insects.
Its robust pelvis, large feet and claws, and strong jaws suggest it foraged near the ground.
Researchers suggest the hoopoe starling's population decline may have been caused by sea-level increases during the last interglacial period, which reduced its habitat on the island.
The hoopoe starling likely nested in tree cavities.
Morioka compared its skull to that of a hoopoe, suggesting it may have fed similarly by probing and making holes in the substrate by inserting and opening its beak.
The hoopoe starling belongs to the kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata, class Aves, order Passeriformes, family Sturnidae, and genus Fregilupus.
Boddaert named it Upupa varia, classifying it in the hoopoe genus, meaning "mottled hoopoe" in reference to its white and dark colors.
Hermann Schlegel proposed in 1857 that the bird belonged to the starling family, reclassifying it as Sturnus capensis.
The genus Fregilupus was named by Lesson in 1831.
The hoopoe starling lived on the island of Réunion and went extinct around 1850.
It was abundant and formed large flocks that inhabited wet areas and swamps.
It lived during the Holocene, from 0.0117 to 0 million years ago.
Andrew John Berger cast doubt on the bird's relationship with starlings in 1957 due to subtle anatomical differences.
A relationship with vangas was proposed by some authors but rejected by Hiroyuki Morioka in 1996.
